 IRS announces 2027 tax changes, higher standard deductions 
 USA TODAY Network via Reuters Connect // November 6, 2026 // 
 Home > News > Money and Labor > IRS announces 2027 tax changes, higher standard deductions
 The IRS warns that viral 'tax hacks' that flourish on social media "can push taxpayers to file returns with false information or claim credits they don’t qualify for, leading to refund delays, audits, penalties, or worse." Source: USA TODAY Network
 IRS announces 2027 tax changes, higher standard deductions 
 USA TODAY Network via Reuters Connect // November 6, 2026 // 
 -->
 Listen to this article 
 KEY TAKEAWAYS: 
 The standard deduction for 2027 increases to $33,200 for married couples filing jointly and $16,600 for single taxpayers.
 Federal income tax brackets will shift upward to account for inflation, potentially reducing tax burdens for some taxpayers.
 The maximum child tax credit rises to $2,300, while the earned income tax credit increases to $8,496 for qualifying families with three or more children.
 Flexible spending account contribution limits increase to $3,500, while the annual gift tax exclusion rises to $20,000.
 The Internal Revenue Service has announced some key inflation-related adjustments for the 2027 tax year involving a long list of tax provisions, including the standard deduction and maximum amount you can save in flexible spending accounts .
 Inflation related adjustments, such as those announced by the IRS on Nov. 5, might help hold down or even slightly lower overall the 2027 tax bill for many people when their returns are due in 2028.
 As inflation has heated up, taxpayers can expect to see some significant changes ahead in the annual inflation adjustment for tax brackets and some tax breaks for 2027. 
 The standard deduction that many people claim when filing their tax returns will be $33,200 for married couples filing jointly in 2027, up $1,000 from 2026.
 Roughly 90% of taxpayers claim the standard deduction now and do not itemize deductions, such as mortgage interest and other deductions.
 For single taxpayers and married individuals filing separately, the standard deduction increases by $500 to hit $16,600 for 2027. For heads of households, the standard deduction will be $24,925 – that’s up $775 from 2026’s standard deduction of $24,150.
 These new adjustments apply to 2027 tax returns, not to the 2026 tax returns that you will file next year. The IRS also updated the marginal tax rates for 2027. Here’s a look at some changes that many people may be watching:
 Flexible spending accounts: The maximum dollar limit that employees can contribute to health flexible spending accounts hits $3,500 in 2027, up $100 from 2026.
 The IRS also noted that the maximum carryover amount will be $700 in 2027, up $20 from 2026, for cafeteria plans that permit the carryover of unused amounts into the following year.
 Child tax credit: The maximum amount of the child tax credit for 2027 will go up by $100 to reach $2,300 in 2027. For tax year 2027, the amount of credit that may be refundable will be $1,800 – up $100 from 2026.
 Earned income tax credit: The maximum earned income tax credit will be $8,496 in 2027 for qualifying taxpayers who have three or more qualifying children. That’s up from a maximum of $8,231 for tax year 2026.
 Annual exclusion for gifts: Some well-off grandparents and others keep an eye on the annual exclusion for gifts, which will increase to $20,000 in 2027, up from $19,000 for calendar year 2026. (The annual exclusion for gifts to a spouse who is not a citizen of the United States increases to $201,000 for calendar year 2027, up from $194,000 for 2026.) This limit is used for estate planning purposes.
 Adoptions: The maximum credit allowed for adoptions for 2027 is the amount of qualified adoption expenses up to $18,250 – a $580 increase from 2026. For tax year 2027, the amount of credit that may be refundable is $5,280.
 The indexing of the marginal tax rate means that a bit more of the money you make in 2027 could end up being taxed at a lower rate. Tax rates remain the same but the income limits that apply to those rates will increase, based on inflation.
 For tax year 2027, the IRS noted, the top tax rate remains 37% for individual single taxpayers with incomes greater than $661,375 or $793,650 for married couples filing jointly. The other rates are:
 35% for incomes over $264,550 ($529,100 for married couples filing jointly);
 32% for incomes over $208,325 ($416,650 for married couples filing jointly);
 24% for incomes over $109,125 ($218,250 for married couples filing jointly);
 22% for incomes over $52,025 ($104,050 for married couples filing jointly);
 12% for incomes over $12,800 ($25,600 for married couples filing jointly).
 Contact personal finance columnist Susan Tompor:  [email protected] . Follow her on X @tompor. 
 This article originally appeared on Detroit Free Press: IRS announces inflation bump for standard deduction and more for 2027 
 Reporting by Susan Tompor, Detroit Free Press / Detroit Free Press
